LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Praying Mantis — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson stands very still and wins: your toddler folds their arms like the mantis on the card, holds the pose one breath longer than seems possible, and meets the garden’s quietest hunter — admired from afar, arms and all.

What is this?

A praying mantis is a tall green insect that stands up on long legs and holds its front arms folded, as if saying hello or thinking hard. It waits without moving for a very long time — then catches its dinner in one quick snap.

What does it mean?

The mantis is the stillness card: every other bug teaches a movement, and this one teaches the absence of it. Toddlers adore a challenge, and stand-still-longer-than-you is the set’s finest quiet contest.

What does the child need to know?

The mantis stands tall with folded arms and waits patiently, and those clever front legs catch bugs — which is exactly why they stay far away from fingers. Watching a real one means standing just as patiently, a little way back.

Why this matters

Holding still on purpose is real self-regulation, and the mantis gives it a hero: a whole animal whose superpower is waiting. The folded arms make the pose copyable, and the quiet makes it a lovely wind-down game.

What it teaches

Stillness and balance as skills in their own right, body imitation (the fold is genuinely tricky), patience with a living model, and the keep-your-distance rule for hunters of any size.

Words to learn

mantisstillarmswaitgreengentle

Say this to your child

“"A praying mantis! See how it stands — arms folded, perfectly still. Can you stand like it? Fold your arms... shhh... hold it... The mantis waits and waits, then catches its dinner. We watch with quiet eyes and our hands stay way back."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and say praying mantis — then fold your arms up like the card: hello, says the mantis, very politely and very still.
  2. Play the copy game: fold arms, stand tall, hold it... and hold it... until somebody giggles. The giggler folds again.
  3. Try the stillness record: how many breaths can the whole family hold the mantis pose? Count them out loud, slowly.
  4. Tell the waiting story: the mantis stands still because it is waiting for its dinner to walk past — patience is its superpower.
  5. End with the rule, quietly: the mantis catches bugs with those front arms, so our fingers stay far away — we watch, we fold our own arms, and we admire.

Look closer at the picture

Say praying mantis together and spot the folded arms on the card — this one is green and standing tall. Make the mantis pose yourself, then ask your toddler to hold it while you count slowly to three.

Ask your child

"What are the mantis’s arms doing?" "Can you stand still like the mantis?" "What is it waiting for?" "Do our fingers go near the mantis’s arms, or stay back?" — answered with a fold, a hush and careful little steps backwards.

What your child can say or do

Arms folded at the dinner table with tremendous dignity, stillness contests instigated against parents and pets, and mantises announced in every tall plant — the garden’s statue has a fan who now stands just as quietly.

Out in the real world

Mantises perch on stems, hedges and flower heads, standing so still they are easy to miss and marvellous to find. Each sighting is a rerun: spot it, fold arms, admire the stillness, and step back kindly.

Try it together

Mantis statues: dance gently around the room until someone calls mantis! — then freeze in the folded-arms pose, tallest and stillest wins. Add a slow breath at the end; even statues need to breathe.

Understanding check

Call the mantis pose at a random moment tomorrow: a frozen, folded, solemn toddler means the card landed — patience arrived on six long legs, and it can be summoned on request.

Parent tips

Join every contest and lose some on purpose — being beaten at stillness by a two-year-old is the funniest, most motivating prize going. Keep the front-leg rule light; a warning said calmly lands better than one said in alarm.

Staying safe

A mantis catches its food with spiky front arms and one quick snap, so real ones are watched from a respectful distance with hands well back. The folded-arms game stays on rugs and grass — statues and hard floors do not mix.

This lesson pairs with the Praying Mantis flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).
